name: Net arrivals from abroad
definition: Net international migration into New York City's five counties in the 12 months ending July 1: people arriving from abroad minus people leaving for abroad, Census Bureau estimate.

source.name: Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program, county population totals and components of change: Vintage 2025 (2021-2025) and Vintage 2020 (2011-2020)

peers.note: Rates are per 1,000 residents for each city's principal county, because the Census Bureau publishes components of change for counties, not cities. New York is the five boroughs combined, which matches the city exactly; Philadelphia, San Francisco, Denver and Washington, D.C. are also coextensive with their counties, and Jacksonville, Indianapolis, Nashville and Boston are close. Elsewhere the county is much larger than the city (Los Angeles, Cook, Harris, Maricopa, Clark, King and others) or the city spills into neighboring counties (Houston, Dallas, Austin, Fort Worth, Oklahoma City, Columbus). Rate = net migrants / average of the July 1 populations at the start and end of the period x 1,000, the Census Bureau's own formula, which this script checks against the published county rates.

source.name: Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 county components of change (published rate columns RINTERNATIONALMIG2025)

values.geo_name: New York City (Bronx, Kings, New York, Queens and Richmond counties), New York
District of Columbia, District of Columbia

method: Sum of the INTERNATIONALMIG<year> columns for the five New York City counties (FIPS 36005, 36047, 36061, 36081, 36085). 2011-2020 from Vintage 2020; 2021-2025 from Vintage 2025. The city series is a count of people. Peer values and peer_series are rates per 1,000 residents, so they are not in the same units as the city series: for the four named peers they are the Census Bureau's published county rates; for New York (included in peer_series so the lines are comparable) the rate is computed from the five-county sums with the Bureau's formula, net migrants / mean of the starting and ending July 1 populations x 1,000. Borough values are counts for July 2024-June 2025.
caveats: Periods run July 1 to June 30 and are labeled by the year they end: '2025' means July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025.

The series joins two vintages. 2011-2020 come from Vintage 2020 (co-est2020-alldata.csv), the last estimates built on the 2010 Census; 2021-2025 come from Vintage 2025 (co-est2025-alldata.csv), built on the 2020 Census. The vintage of every year is recorded in its series point. The Vintage 2020 components used for 2011-2020 were not revised to agree with the 2020 Census.
Partial periods are left out: Vintage 2020's '2010' column covers only April 1 to July 1, 2010, and Vintage 2025's '2020' column covers only April 1 to July 1, 2020.
Components of change are modeled estimates, not counts, and are revised with every vintage. They carry no published margin of error.

Vintage 2024 changed the method for net international migration, adding administrative data on humanitarian and other recent arrivals, and its estimates for 2022-2024 were much higher than earlier vintages had shown. Vintage 2025 revises every year from 2021 on. Years 2011-2020 come from Vintage 2020, which used the older method, so part of the jump after 2021 reflects a change in measurement, not only a change in arrivals.
Net international migration includes net movement between the United States and Puerto Rico.

Rates are per 1,000 residents for each city's principal county, because the Census Bureau publishes components of change for counties, not cities. New York is the five boroughs combined, which matches the city exactly; Philadelphia, San Francisco, Denver and Washington, D.C. are also coextensive with their counties, and Jacksonville, Indianapolis, Nashville and Boston are close. Elsewhere the county is much larger than the city (Los Angeles, Cook, Harris, Maricopa, Clark, King and others) or the city spills into neighboring counties (Houston, Dallas, Austin, Fort Worth, Oklahoma City, Columbus). Rate = net migrants / average of the July 1 populations at the start and end of the period x 1,000, the Census Bureau's own formula, which this script checks against the published county rates.
